criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly explains the two mechanisms behind the monolith's decay (tool-selection space growth and context/trajectory bloat), describes the orchestrator/worker pattern and context isolation accurately, and states true trade-offs (token multiplication per hop, latency dependent on parallelisability, multiplicative reliability). No false claims (e.g. that multi-agent is inherently cheaper, that agents share state implicitly, or that parallelism always cuts latency). Deduct for each mechanism that is vague, mislabelled, or wrong.

Full marks: covers all five required strands — diagnosis, recommended topology and its benefit, an explicit lead/worker context-passing contract, cost/latency/reliability trade-offs, and named conditions for rejecting multi-agent with cheaper alternatives. Deduct for each strand missing or addressed only superficially (e.g. proposes the topology but never states the context contract, or lists no condition under which multi-agent is the wrong choice).

Full marks: recommendations are justified by mechanism and tied to the symptoms in the scenario (fills window -> isolate context; wrong-tool -> narrow tool sets), trade-offs are weighed rather than asserted, and the decision to split or not is contingent on task coupling/parallelisability rather than a blanket preference. Deduct where claims are asserted without cause-and-effect reasoning.

Full marks: organised as a reviewable assessment, uses correct vocabulary (orchestrator/supervisor, worker/sub-agent, context isolation, blackboard/shared store, tool-RAG, ReAct) precisely, and is concise and unambiguous. Deduct for disorganised structure, hand-wavy jargon used without meaning, or an answer a reader could not act on.

expected_answer_points: Diagnoses the monolith's failure as structural: 25 tools enlarge the per-step tool-selection space (degrading tool choice and inflating the system prompt) AND the single long trajectory bloats the context window, diluting attention and raising latency/cost.

Recommends an orchestrator/supervisor-worker topology where a lead agent decomposes and delegates to specialised sub-agents, each scoped to a small relevant tool subset, and identifies context isolation (and per-agent evaluability) as the core benefit.

Specifies a context-passing contract: workers get only their relevant slice and return condensed structured results/artifacts (not raw transcripts); large artifacts passed by reference/handle via a shared store; no broadcasting of full message history.

Quantifies the cost/latency trade-off: multi-agent multiplies token usage because each hop re-reads context/instructions and adds round-trips (often several-fold, e.g. Anthropic's ~15x), and parallelism only helps wall-clock latency when sub-tasks are independent — sequential delegation adds latency.

Addresses reliability/failure isolation: end-to-end reliability compounds across hops, so the orchestrator must validate outputs, use timeouts/retries, and contain sub-agent failures so errors/hallucinations don't propagate downstream.

States explicit conditions to reject multi-agent: tightly coupled/stateful sequential tasks coordinate poorly through message passing (favouring a single-threaded agent with context compression), and tool-ambiguity/retrieval problems are better solved by cheaper fixes (better tool descriptions, tool grouping/namespacing, tool-RAG, or an intra-agent routing classifier).
Notes the added evaluation/observability burden: per-agent plus end-to-end tracing and eval are now required, and the system is harder to debug and more non-deterministic.
common_pitfalls: Treats multi-agent as strictly better or 'more scalable' and ignores the token/latency multiplier and the new coordination failure modes it introduces.

Proposes passing each worker's full transcript or broadcasting the entire conversation history to every sub-agent, which re-bloats context and destroys the isolation benefit the refactor was meant to deliver.
Assumes sub-agents coordinate implicitly over shared state, when they communicate only via explicit messages — so on a coupled/sequential task they produce conflicting or duplicated work.
Jumps straight to multi-agent without considering cheaper single-agent fixes first (sharper tool descriptions, tool grouping/namespacing, tool-RAG, or a routing classifier inside one agent).

Conflates multi-agent (many coordinating agents) with multi-model routing (one agent over a model cascade), or claims parallelism always lowers latency while ignoring task dependencies and the aggregation/merge cost.
Ignores reliability compounding across hops and offers no output validation, timeout/retry, failure-containment, or per-agent evaluation strategy.
reference_answer:
Diagnosis first. The monolith degrades for two compounding, structural reasons, not because the code is untidy. (1) Decision-space blowup: all 25 tool descriptions live in the system prompt, so at every step the model must discriminate among 25 options — tool-selection accuracy falls and the prompt is large before any work begins. (2) Trajectory bloat: a single long thread accumulates every observation, so effective context grows unbounded, diluting attention, hurting instruction-following, and driving up both latency and token cost until the window fills. Evaluation is hard because there is exactly one opaque trajectory to attribute failures to.

Recommended topology: an orchestrator (supervisor)/worker pattern. A lead agent decomposes the request and delegates sub-tasks to specialised sub-agents — e.g. a search agent, a SQL agent, a writer — each with a scoped system prompt and a small, relevant subset of the 25 tools. The primary benefit is context isolation: each worker reasons over a narrow tool set and only its slice of context, which restores tool-choice accuracy and shortens trajectories, and each worker becomes independently evaluable. It does NOT, by itself, fix bad retrieval, ambiguous tool descriptions, or a genuinely sequential task.

Context-passing contract (this matters more than the box diagram). Each sub-agent receives only the slice it needs, and must return a condensed, structured result (a summary or artifact), not its raw transcript — otherwise the orchestrator's context re-bloats with every worker's full trace and you have recreated the monolith one level up. Large artifacts (tables, documents, images) are passed by reference/handle through a shared store or blackboard and only the handle is inlined. Do not broadcast the whole message history to every agent.

Trade-offs. Multi-agent is not free. Each hop re-reads instructions and context, and orchestration adds round-trips, so token spend multiplies — often several-fold (Anthropic reported ~15x versus a single chat for their research system). You only earn that back when sub-tasks are independent enough to run in parallel, cutting wall-clock latency; purely sequential delegation just adds latency and cost. Reliability compounds multiplicatively across hops (end-to-end success is roughly the product of per-step success rates), so the orchestrator must validate worker outputs, apply timeouts/retries, and contain a failing sub-agent rather than let a hallucinated or malformed result propagate downstream. You also now need per-agent plus end-to-end tracing and eval.

When to reject multi-agent. If the task is tightly coupled and stateful — later steps depend on earlier reasoning — agents coordinate badly because they share nothing implicitly and communicate only by messages, producing conflicting or duplicated work; here a single-threaded agent with context compression is the better call. And if the real failure is tool ambiguity or retrieval, cheaper fixes come first: sharper tool descriptions, grouping/namespacing tools, retrieving tools by relevance (tool-RAG), or a routing classifier inside one agent. Reach for multi-agent only when sub-tasks are genuinely separable, parallelisable, or require different context or policies.
